name: Marco Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything's confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm the farm lead at Kestrel Farm, which is about 400 hectares of potatoes, oilseed rape and wheat, with six hundred ewes on the grass leys in between. I do the crop side, the sheep when it's lambing, and all the tech, which means the GPS on the tractors, the soil maps and the drone. Typical day, I'm flying the drone over the potatoes at eight to check for blight, then I'm on a tractor, then I'm on the phone to the agronomist.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Sounds like you're the tech person there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty much. I use AI tools every day, for spray plans, for reading the drone images, even for writing the grain contracts in plain language for the boss, Mr Hale. I like it, it's like having a very fast intern. The downside is I'm paid like a farmhand, not a tech guy, and I'm renting a flat above the bakery in the village with almost nothing saved. Single, so at least it's only my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still useful, just not magic. I'd post something like 'AI won't drive your tractor, but it'll tell you where the blight is'. At work I'd keep showing Mr Hale little wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little let down, but it's fine for me. It means my job stays, my skills stay a bit ahead of other farm workers, and nobody comes for me. The problem is still the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, use the tools I use. I'd probably start doing drone mapping for two or three neighbouring farms on the side, charging per hectare, maybe on Saturdays. That would help with the savings, which is basically nothing right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit underwhelmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Drone mapping on the side. Have you priced that out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roughly. If I did three farms a month, that's maybe a few hundred extra. Mr Hale pays me to fly his drone, and the neighbours would pay me to fly it over their fields on my day off. I'd need my own drone eventually, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the side work took off, would you leave Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this picture. There's not enough work round here to live off it alone. I'd keep both and see.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still useful, just not magic, and joke online that it won't drive your tractor but will find your blight. At work I'd keep showing the boss small wins.
S0.think: I'd be a little let down, but it's fine for me, because my job and my edge over other farm workers stay. The problem is still the money.
S0.do: Keeps using his everyday AI tools and starts drone mapping for two or three neighbouring farms on Saturdays, charging per hectare. Plans to buy his own drone eventually.
S0.quote: Mr Hale pays me to fly his drone, and the neighbours would pay me to fly it over their fields on my day off.
S0.fieldNote: He likes the tools and sees value in them even in the dull version of the future. His answer to low pay is to sell his tech skill on the side. He's realistic that the local market isn't big enough to go solo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it, but sensibly. Some jobs will go, but farming's short of people anyway. I'd tell people at the young farmers' club to learn the kit now rather than complain later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is mostly good for me. I'm the one on the farm who knows how the robots and the software talk to each other. If anything, it should make me harder to replace, and maybe better paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd push Mr Hale to trial a self-driving tractor kit on the potato ground next season. I'd ask for a pay rise to match, because I'd be running it. And I'd build the drone side business into a proper little service for the valley, maybe with a second-hand spray drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually a bit excited. Like the first day of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it should make you better paid. What if Mr Hale says no to the rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look around, because in this picture people like me get asked for. For once I'd be the scarce one, not the sheep. I'd give him a chance first though, he's been decent to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two tractor drivers, Lewis and old Sid. Lewis is young, he'd adapt. Sid I'd worry about, he's got four years till retirement, and I'd hope Mr Hale lets him finish on the sheep side.

S1.say: I'd say let's get on with it, sensibly, since farming's short of people anyway. I'd tell the young farmers' club to learn the kit now.
S1.think: I think this is mostly good for me, because I'm the one who knows how the robots and software talk to each other. It should make me harder to replace.
S1.do: Pushes his boss to trial a self-driving tractor kit on the potato ground next season and asks for a raise to run it. Builds his drone service into a proper business for the valley, maybe with a second-hand spray drone.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the first day of harvest.
S1.quote: For once I'd be the scarce one, not the sheep.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an opportunity that turns his tech habits into bargaining power. He'd use that power for pay but stays loyal to a decent boss. His worry for an older colleague near retirement is specific and kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the bigger ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy and we need some kind of plan from the government quick. I'm not one to shout, but I'd say that openly. I'd also say to people, learn what you can now, because in two years it's too late to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my advantage lasts maybe a year. If the AI can set itself up and fix itself, nobody needs a farm tech guy. And I've got basically nothing saved and a flat above a bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on learning the new systems, right now, every evening. I'd try to get a job with whichever company is rolling the robots out to farms, installing and training farmers, even if it means moving to the city. And I'd cut right back, sell my motorbike, live cheap, save what I can for the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I'd have something to do, but properly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to the city. How would that feel for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. I grew up two villages over. I'd be teaching farmers to trust the robot that just took my job, in a company polo shirt. I'd do it though, for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One good year to get in early with the robot companies. That's all, but it's something. Without it I'd be just another farm worker looking for a job.

S2.say: I'd say this will be messy and we need a quick government plan. I'd tell people to learn what they can now, because in two years it's too late to start.
S2.think: My advantage lasts maybe a year, because if AI sets itself up nobody needs a farm tech guy. I've got nothing saved and a flat above a bakery.
S2.do: Spends every evening learning the new systems and applies to the companies rolling out farm robots, as an installer and trainer, even if it means moving to the city. Sells his motorbike and lives cheaply to save for the gap.
S2.feel: Properly anxious but not panicked, because he has something to do.
S2.quote: I'd be teaching farmers to trust the robot that just took my job, in a company polo shirt.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture he moves towards the technology, not away. He admits the irony of selling robots to farmers in a company polo shirt. His thin savings make the short window feel tight despite his adaptability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people who get going now. I'd say farms should be training their own people on this, not just hiring from outside. That's what I'd say at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a decent run for me. I can build the drone and robot service into something real in the valley, then sell it or fold it into a bigger company when AGI arrives. I'd be thirty-two, with five years of something to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd buy a second-hand spray drone on finance and register the business. I'd keep my job at Kestrel part-time if Mr Hale agreed. And I'd do an online course in robot maintenance, so I can service other people's kit, not just fly drones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, but more focused than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a drone on finance with almost no savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. If a few jobs fall through I'm in trouble. I'd be betting my rent on the weather and on farmers paying their invoices on time, which is a brave bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd be working for someone else, with five I could build my own thing. That's a big difference for me. I'd rather own a small business that gets swallowed than never have one.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people who get going now, and farms should train their own people. That's what I'd say at the young farmers' club.
S3.think: Five years is a decent run, enough to build a drone and robot service in the valley and then sell it or join a bigger company. I'd be thirty-two with something to show.
S3.do: Buys a second-hand spray drone on finance in the first year and registers the business, keeping his farm job part-time if allowed. Takes an online course in robot maintenance to service other people's machines.
S3.feel: Uneasy at the back of his mind but more focused than worried.
S3.quote: I'd be betting my rent on the weather and on farmers paying their invoices on time, which is a brave bet.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time shifts him from employee to owner, which clearly matters to him. He's honest that the finance risk is real with no savings. He thinks of the business as something to build and later sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. People should start learning bits now, slowly, and the government should help with costs for small farms. I'd be pretty upbeat about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best one for me. Ten years to build a real business, learn properly, maybe even buy a bit of land when older farmers sell. By thirty-seven I could have something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the drone service next spring, grow it slowly, and only buy kit when I've got the contracts to pay for it. I'd stay at Kestrel full-time for the first couple of years. And I'd try to save properly, maybe a hundred a month at first, then more as the business picks up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite optimistic, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying land. Is that a real hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a long shot. But if robots do the work, a small farm might pay again for someone who knows the kit. My granddad sold his last field in 1998, and I'd love to be the one who buys a field back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get too comfortable and not move. Ten years feels long, and then suddenly it's year eight. So I'd want to set myself proper goals each year.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses: start learning now, and the government should help small farms with costs. I'd be upbeat in public.
S4.think: This is the best one for me: ten years to build a real business, learn properly and maybe buy land when older farmers sell. By thirty-seven I could have something solid.
S4.do: Starts the drone service next spring and only buys kit once contracts can pay for it, while staying full-time at the farm for two years. Saves about a hundred a month at first and more as the business grows.
S4.quote: My granddad sold his last field in 1998, and I'd love to be the one who buys a field back.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he's at his most hopeful and most careful, buying kit only when work is secured. The grandfather's field gives his ambition a personal root. His worry is about his own complacency, not the technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole edge is being early, and two years doesn't leave room to be early. What would help is cheap loans for young people starting small farm-tech businesses, and some kind of rent support for the gap. Being good with new tech only helps if the new tech gives you time to use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who repairs all these robots in a muddy field in February. Everyone imagines them working in sunshine. Somebody will still be crawling under one in the rain, at least for a while.

headlineQuote: Being good with new tech only helps if the new tech gives you time to use it.
portrait: Marco Schmidt is a 27-year-old farm lead on a potato, oilseed and sheep farm, single, renting a flat above the village bakery with almost no savings and farmhand pay despite his degree. He's pragmatic, centre-ground, and uses AI tools every day, running the farm's GPS and drone. He's calm if AI is hype and even excited by steady change, which would make him the scarce one. AGI in two years makes him anxious because his edge only lasts a year, so he'd move to the city to install robots for a company. With five or ten years he plans to build his own drone and robot service, and dreams of buying back a field like the one his grandfather sold.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his edge is being early and two years leaves no room for it.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for young people starting small farm-tech businesses and rent support during the gap.
